title: The Journey of the Queen of the South: Sheba to Jerusalem and Home
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: The Incense Kingdom: the Queen's Realm

stops.name: Marib, the Sabaean capital and the Great Dam
stops.campa: In the red land between the deserts stands Marib, seat of Saba, where the wadi Dhana is bridled by a wall of earth and stone longer than a marching army: the Great Dam that turns flood into orchard. Two sluices breathe water into a green oasis; palm and vine and grain rise where sand should be. The queen's storehouses hold gold from the south and the pale tears of the incense trees. Almaqah the god is worshipped; the sun is honored in the high places. From here the caravan roads run north to the sea of nations.
stops.quote: Indeed, I found [there] a woman ruling them, and she has been given of all things, and she has a great throne.
suggested_refs: Ruins of the Great Marib Dam and its sluice gates, Yemen
Sabaean inscriptions of Marib

stops.name: The Temple of Awwam (Mahram Bilqis), Marib
stops.campa: South of the city, ringed by a great oval wall, stands the sanctuary the later ages will call Mahram Bilqis: the Sanctuary of the Queen. Here Almaqah, the moon-bull of Saba, receives frankincense on his altars; pilgrims process between eight tall pillars into the sacred oval. The queen makes offering as her fathers did, mistress of a people who worship the host of heaven. Yet a rumor travels the incense roads with the caravans: that in the north a king named Solomon knows the speech of birds and the names of God.
stops.quote: I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah, and Satan has made their deeds pleasing to them.
suggested_refs: Temple of Awwam (Mahram Bilqis) oval precinct and pillars, Marib
Statue offerings to Almaqah, Sabaean bronze

stops.name: The Frankincense Groves of Dhofar
stops.campa: Eastward along the incense coast the Boswellia trees grow from bare rock, wounded by the harvesters' blades so that the wound weeps a milky resin that hardens into pearls of frankincense. This is the treasure the whole known world burns before its gods: Egypt, Babylon, Israel. The queen's wealth is smoke: the roads that carry it, the wells that water it, the wall of Marib that feeds the men who walk it. She resolves to bring this treasure herself to the throne of the king who has heard of her god.
suggested_refs: Frankincense trees (Boswellia sacra), Wadi Dawkah, Oman
Land of Frankincense UNESCO caravan sites

stops.name: Aksum, the Ethiopian Throne of Makeda
stops.campa: Across the strait, in the highlands of Ethiopia, the same queen sits, for the Kebra Nagast keeps her here, Makeda, ruler of a realm that reaches from Aksum to the incense sea. Her merchant Tamrin returns from the north drunk with wonder at Solomon's wisdom and justice, at the palace he builds for the God of Israel. Makeda listens, and a fire kindles in her: she will not send tribute, she will go herself. She commands the caravan made ready: camels beyond counting, gold, gems, and the frankincense of the south.
stops.quote: I am smitten with the love of wisdom... for wisdom is far better than treasure of gold and silver, and wisdom is the best of everything that hath been created on the earth.
stops.quote_source: Kebra Nagast, ch. 24 (Budge), Makeda resolves to journey
suggested_refs: Stelae field of Aksum (Obelisk of Aksum)
Dungur 'Palace of the Queen of Sheba' ruins, Aksum

segments.name: The Hoopoe's Errand: the Bird Between Two Thrones

stops.name: Solomon's Court, the Muster of the Birds
stops.campa: In Jerusalem, Solomon, to whom God has taught the speech of birds and given command over wind and jinn, reviews his winged host. He finds one place empty. 'Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent? I will surely punish him or slaughter him, unless he brings me clear authority.' The ranks of the birds stand silent under the king's anger; the small brown crested bird is nowhere in the sky. Then, from the south, a shape comes beating over the desert with news.
stops.quote: And he inspected the birds and said, 'Why do I not see the hoopoe — or is he among the absent? I will surely punish him with a severe punishment or slaughter him unless he brings me clear authorization.'
suggested_refs: Persian miniature of Solomon enthroned among birds and jinn
Hoopoe (Upupa epops) in Islamic manuscript illumination

stops.name: The Hoopoe's Report of Saba
stops.campa: The hoopoe alights and speaks without fear: 'I have encompassed that which you have not, and I have come to you from Saba with certain news.' He tells of a woman who rules there, given every good thing, with a mighty throne, but he found her and her people bowing to the sun, turned by Satan from the way of God. Solomon does not strike the bird. 'We will see,' he says, 'whether you were truthful or were of the liars.' He writes a letter and seals it, and gives it into the beak of the bird.
stops.quote: I have encompassed [in knowledge] that which you have not encompassed, and I have come to you from Saba with certain news.
suggested_refs: Bilqis and the hoopoe, Persian/Mughal drawing (Google Arts & Culture)
Falnama illustration of Solomon and the hoopoe

stops.name: The Letter in the Bird's Beak, delivered to the Queen
stops.campa: The hoopoe flies south and drops the sealed letter into the queen's own court. She takes it up and reads it aloud to her chiefs: 'A noble letter has been delivered to me. It is from Solomon, and it is: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Be not haughty with me, but come to me in submission.' The words are few and the summons is total: not to tribute but to God. The queen, wise, will not answer alone.
stops.quote: Indeed, it is from Solomon, and indeed, it reads: 'In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Be not haughty with me but come to me in submission [as Muslims].'
suggested_refs: Ottoman/Persian miniature: the hoopoe delivering Solomon's letter to Bilqis
Calligraphic 'Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim' panel

segments.name: The Queen's Counsel: the Gift Before the Journey

stops.name: The Council of the Chiefs, Saba
stops.campa: The queen sets the matter before her lords: 'O eminent ones, advise me in my affair. I would not decide a matter until you witness for me.' They answer that they are strong and fierce in war, yet the command is hers. She is wiser than her warriors. 'Indeed kings, when they enter a city, ruin it and render the honored of its people humbled. And thus do they do.' She will not meet strength with strength. First she will test him: send a gift, and watch what the messengers bring back.
stops.quote: Indeed kings — when they enter a city, they ruin it and render the honored of its people humbled. And thus do they do.
suggested_refs: Sabaean throne-hall reconstruction, Marib
South Arabian alabaster relief of a seated ruler

stops.name: The Testing Gift Sent to Solomon
stops.campa: She sends a rich present ahead by envoys. But when it reaches Solomon he is unmoved and stern: 'Do you provide me with wealth? What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you. Rather, it is you who rejoice in your gift.' He bids the envoy return, with a threat of hosts the queen cannot withstand, and expulsion in disgrace. The message is unmistakable: this king wants no gold. He wants the queen herself, and her surrender to God. Now she knows she must go north in person.
stops.quote: Do you provide me with wealth? But what Allah has given me is better than what He has given you. Rather, it is you who rejoice in your gift.
suggested_refs: Sabaean gold and incense trade goods, South Arabian museum pieces

segments.name: The Great Caravan North: the Incense Road

stops.name: Najran, the Parting of the Roads
stops.campa: The caravan sets out along the incense road, and the first great oasis is Najran, where the north and south routes divide among the palms. Camels beyond number bear the queen's treasure: gold, gems, and above all the spices, so much frankincense that no such quantity of it will ever come again. Wells are drawn, beasts are watered, guides are hired for the long dry stages ahead. The queen rides toward a king she has never seen, carrying with her the hard questions she has prepared to prove him.
stops.quote: She came to Jerusalem with a very great train, with camels that bare spices, and very much gold, and precious stones.
suggested_refs: Najran oasis and Al-Ukhdud ruins, Saudi Arabia
Camel caravan of the Incense Route (relief / illustration)

stops.name: Dedan (Al-'Ula), the Oasis Waystation
stops.campa: Weeks into the wilderness the road threads the sandstone canyons of Dedan, green with date-gardens fed by hidden springs. Here the caravans of all the incense lands rest and trade under the cliffs. The queen's train, with its dark tents, kneeling camels, and smoke of cook-fires, draws the desert's eyes. She hears again, at every well, the fame of Solomon joined to the name of the LORD his God, and the reports only sharpen her resolve to see with her own eyes whether the half of it is true.
stops.quote: And when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to prove him with hard questions.
suggested_refs: Dedan / Lihyanite ruins and lion tombs, Al-'Ula
Hegra (Mada'in Salih) rock-cut tombs nearby

stops.name: Tayma, the Great Desert Well
stops.campa: At Tayma, oldest of the northern oases, the famed well and its ringed wall sustain the caravan across the edge of the Nafud sands. The queen rehearses her riddles in the cool of the tents: the questions she will lay before the king to catch his wisdom, of which the whole road speaks. Ahead lie Petra's ravines and the highlands of Judah. The frankincense goes on ahead of her like a promise of smoke; she comes behind it, a queen bearing the wealth of the south to the city of the God of Israel.
suggested_refs: Tayma well and ancient city wall, Saudi Arabia
Tayma stele and Aramaic inscriptions

segments.name: Jerusalem: the Meeting of the Two Thrones

stops.name: The Arrival at Solomon's Jerusalem
stops.campa: The caravan climbs at last into the hill-city of David, and the queen enters Jerusalem with her very great train. The Temple stands new upon its mount; the king's cedar palace, the House of the Forest of Lebanon, gleams. She comes before Solomon and communes with him of all that is in her heart, holding back nothing. She lays out her hard questions one by one, the riddles she carried across a thousand miles of desert, and waits to see whether any thing can be hidden from this king.
stops.quote: And when she was come to Solomon, she communed with him of all that was in her heart.
suggested_refs: Solomon's Temple reconstruction models
Tintoretto / Veronese, The Queen of Sheba before Solomon

stops.name: The Riddles Answered
stops.campa: Solomon answers all her questions; there is not any thing hid from the king which he tells her not. In the aggadah she brings sharper snares still: children dressed alike, boys and girls to be told apart; flowers real and artificial that only the bees betray; the water that is neither rain nor spring but the sweat of a labored horse. Each riddle he unknots. The queen who came to prove him is proven; the fame that crossed the desert falls short of the man before her. Her spirit fails within her.
stops.quote: And Solomon told her all her questions: there was not any thing hid from the king, which he told her not.
suggested_refs: Targum Sheni to Esther (the riddles of the Queen)
Midrash Mishlei (Midrash on Proverbs) riddle-list

stops.name: The Glass Floor of the Throne-Court
stops.campa: Solomon has her led into a pavilion whose floor is a smooth expanse of crystal, water gleaming beneath it. 'Enter the palace,' he says. Taking it for a pool, she bares her legs to wade, and the king sees. 'It is a palace whose floor is made smooth with glass,' he tells her. In the aggadah he speaks of the hair upon her legs: beautiful in a man, unseemly in a woman, and the jinn are set to make her a depilatory. The trick that shames her is the trick that turns her: the marvel is real, and so is the God who taught the king to make it.
stops.quote: It was said to her, 'Enter the palace.' But when she saw it, she thought it was a body of water and uncovered her shins. He said, 'Indeed, it is a palace whose floor is made smooth with glass.'
suggested_refs: Persian miniature: Bilqis lifting her skirt on the crystal floor
Piero di Cosimo / Renaissance panels of the glass pavement

stops.name: 'The Half Was Not Told Me'
stops.campa: She has seen it all: the wisdom, the house he built, the food of his table, the sitting of his servants, the ascent by which he goes up to the House of the LORD, and there is no more spirit in her. She confesses that the report she heard in her own land was a true report, and yet she believed not until she came and her own eyes had seen. The reality outruns every rumor. She blesses the LORD his God, who set him on the throne of Israel to do judgment and justice.
stops.quote: Howbeit I believed not the words, until I came, and mine eyes had seen it: and, behold, the half was not told me: thy wisdom and prosperity exceedeth the fame which I heard.
suggested_refs: 1 Kings 10 illuminated Bible pages
Edward Poynter, The Visit of the Queen of Sheba to King Solomon

stops.name: The Queen Submits to the God of Israel
stops.campa: The sun-worshipper turns. In the Quran she says at the crystal floor: 'My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I submit with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds.' In the Kebra Nagast she declares it plainly to the king: from this hour she will not worship the sun but the Creator of the sun, the God of Israel. Two scriptures, one conversion: the queen who came bearing incense for the host of heaven kneels now to the One who made the heaven. The gifts are exchanged; the meeting has done its work.
stops.quote: My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I submit with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
suggested_refs: Kebra Nagast manuscript (Ge'ez), Makeda's confession
'From this moment I will worship the Creator of the sun', Kebra Nagast ch. 28

segments.name: The Night of the Oath: the Conception of Menelik

stops.name: The Oath and the Salted Feast
stops.campa: On the eve of her departure, the Kebra Nagast tells, Solomon prepares a feast heavy with spices and salt, and bids the queen sleep in his chamber. She fears him; he swears an oath: 'I will not take thee by force, but swear thou wilt take nothing by force that is in my house.' She swears it, lightly, a queen who wants for nothing. The lamps are lowered. He has set, near her bed, a single bowl of water where the fire's heat will find it in the deep of the salted night.
stops.quote: I will swear to thee that I will not take thee by force, but thou must swear to me that thou wilt not take by force anything that is in my house.
suggested_refs: Kebra Nagast illuminated manuscript pages, Ethiopia
Ethiopian church mural of Solomon and Makeda

stops.name: The Water Taken, the Oath Broken
stops.campa: In the dark she wakes parched, her throat burning from the salt. She rises and lifts the bowl to drink. At once the king's hand closes on hers. 'Why hast thou broken thine oath, that thou wouldst take nothing by force that is in my house?' Water, he says, is the freest and best of all things, and she has taken it. Released from her word, she is his; that night the queen conceives. He gives her a ring: a token, that any son she bears may one day come and be known to his father by it.
stops.quote: Why hast thou broken the oath that thou hast sworn that thou wouldst not take by force anything that is in my house?
suggested_refs: The ring of Solomon (Seal of Solomon) motif
Kebra Nagast ch. 30-31 manuscript

stops.name: The Wooden Bridge, the Sibyl and the Cross
stops.campa: In the medieval legend of the True Cross the queen becomes a Sibyl, a seer. Coming to a stream she finds a beam laid down for a bridge: timber Solomon felled from the holy tree grown on Adam's grave, wood that would serve for nothing else. She will not set foot upon it. She kneels in the dust and adores it, for in a flash she sees the Savior of the world who will one day hang upon that very wood. She tells the king: his glory shall be undone by One crucified upon this beam.
suggested_refs: Piero della Francesca, 'The Queen of Sheba Adoring the Wood', San Francesco, Arezzo
Jacobus de Voragine, Golden Legend, the Exaltation of the Cross

segments.name: The Homeward Road: the Birth of the Son

stops.name: The Return South with Solomon's Gifts
stops.campa: Solomon gives to the queen of his royal bounty, all her desire, whatsoever she asks, beside that which he gives of his own hand. Laden now with the wisdom and wealth of Israel, she turns her camels home down the same incense road, past Petra's rose ravines, toward the sea and the southern kingdoms. She carries more than gifts: a ring, an oath broken, and a child quickening in her. The desert that bore her north bears her home again, a different queen than the one who came.
stops.quote: And king Solomon gave unto the queen of Sheba all her desire, whatsoever she asked, beside that which Solomon gave her of his royal bounty. So she turned and went to her own country, she and her servants.
suggested_refs: Petra (the Nabataean city on the incense road)
Claude Lorrain, 'Seaport with the Embarkation of the Queen of Sheba'

stops.name: The Birth of Menelik on the Road
stops.campa: On the long way home, in the borderlands of her own country, the queen is delivered of a son. She names him Baynā-Leḥkem, whom the ages will call Menelik: the child of the wise king. She raises him in her highland realm as a prince of the God of Israel, and he grows tall and kingly, the very image of Solomon. Always he asks after his father; and his mother keeps the ring against the day he is old enough to cross the desert and stand before the throne in Jerusalem.
suggested_refs: Kebra Nagast ch. 32 (the birth of the son)
Ethiopian icon of Menelik I

stops.name: Aksum, the Queen's Highland Throne Regained
stops.campa: The caravan climbs at last into the stone highlands of Aksum, home. The queen resumes her throne, and it is here, in the Kebra Nagast's telling, that she rules as Makeda, mother of a dynasty not yet born. She has changed the faith of her people: the sun is dethroned, the God of Israel enthroned. The boy Menelik grows to manhood in this city of stelae, hearing always of the far Jerusalem where a king who is his father sits in glory, and of the House of God upon its mountain.
stops.quote: And the Queen departed and came into the country of Bâlâ Zadîsârĕyâ nine months and five days after she had separated from King Solomon.
suggested_refs: Great Stele of Aksum
Dungur (Queen of Sheba's Palace), Aksum

segments.name: The Son's Return: the Ark Comes to Aksum

stops.name: Menelik's Journey to Jerusalem by Way of Gaza
stops.campa: Grown to two-and-twenty, Menelik crosses the deserts his mother crossed, coming up to Jerusalem by way of Gaza. He carries the ring. Men marvel at the road, for his face is Solomon's face; some cry that the king walks among them, though the king sits in his palace. Brought before the throne, the young man draws out the token. Solomon knows it and knows him, and embraces the son of the queen of the south, anoints him king, and names him David after his grandfather, king of the land of Ethiopia.
suggested_refs: Gaza on the incense road to the Levant
Kebra Nagast ch. 33-38 (Menelik before Solomon)

stops.name: The Taking of Zion, the Ark Carried Off
stops.campa: Solomon sends the firstborn sons of his elders to attend the young king home. But Azariah, son of the high priest, cannot bear to leave the Ark of Zion behind. By night, the Kebra Nagast tells, an angel guides them; they lift Zion, the Tabernacle of the Law of God, from its place and set carved wood where it stood. Menelik learns of it only when it is too late to return, and sees that God Himself wills it, for the caravan is carried as on wings, the wagons riding a span above the earth all the way south.
stops.quote: And the four of them carried Zion away, and they brought it into the house of Azaryas, and they went back into the house of God, and they set the pieces of wood [there] where Zion had been.
suggested_refs: The Ark of the Covenant (Tabot) in Ethiopian tradition
Kebra Nagast ch. 45-52 manuscript illuminations

stops.name: The Ark Enthroned at Aksum: the Lion of Judah
stops.campa: The Ark comes home to Aksum, borne through the highlands to the city of the queen. Makeda welcomes her son with feasting and abdicates her throne to him; Menelik I reigns, and the Ark of Zion rests in Ethiopia. From this union of Solomon and the queen of the south springs the Solomonic dynasty, the line of the Lion of the Tribe of Judah, that will hold the throne of Ethiopia into the age of chronicles. Where the queen once burned incense to the sun, the Glory of Zion now dwells among her children.
stops.quote: And they shall bring the Tabernacle of the Law of God... and it shall be in the country of Ethiopia.
stops.quote_source: Kebra Nagast (the prophecy of Zion's dwelling in Ethiopia)
suggested_refs: Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion and the Chapel of the Tablet, Aksum
Lion of Judah emblem of the Ethiopian Solomonic dynasty
